implementation_notes: Swift's baseline is explicit injection: a view or type receives what it needs through its initializer (`struct UserCard: View { let user: User }`), which keeps it constructible in isolation and previewable, and value semantics make the copied-along values cheap. The smell appears when container views declare values they only pass on to their children; keep this default while the tree is shallow and the value is local.
pitfalls: Deep initializer chains make previews verbose: every container in a SwiftUI preview must be given values it does not use.
Memberwise initializers generated by the compiler change when a relayed property is added, breaking call sites in every container along the chain.

variants.name: SwiftUI environment values
variants.implementation_notes: SwiftUI's scoped-consumption mechanism: a value is written into a view's environment with `.environment(\.keyPath, value)` (custom keys via `EnvironmentKey`/`EnvironmentValues`) and any descendant reads it with `@Environment(\.keyPath)`, so container views never declare it - the framework walks the view hierarchy. This is the documented replacement for threading values through containers; it suits widely used, mostly read-only context (color scheme, locale, shared model objects) and hides the dependency from the initializer, which previews and tests must re-provide.
pitfalls: A missing environment value falls back to the key's default (commonly nil) silently; guard in the consumer or document a non-optional default.
Environment values are per presentation hierarchy: sheets, popovers and new windows do not automatically inherit a custom environment from the presenting view in the way a child view does.

variants.name: TaskLocal values for structured concurrency
variants.implementation_notes: For structured-concurrency code, the standard library provides task-local values: an `@TaskLocal static var` is bound with `$value.withValue(...) { ... }` and is implicitly carried to child tasks (`async let`, task groups), so request-scoped data reaches awaited code without being threaded through every async function. The binding is scoped and reverts when the closure ends, which avoids the thread-leak problem of thread-local storage; the documentation notes that the value is implicitly carried with the task and readable by child tasks.
pitfalls: Work dispatched outside the `withValue` scope (a detached `Task`, a delegate callback) does not see the value; detached tasks start from the root context.
Task locals are read-only within their scope - a consumer that needs to update request state must use an explicit parameter or an actor.
